implementation_notes: Swift's AsyncSequence is the splitter: a type that vends parts one at a time conforms to AsyncSequence/AsyncIteratorProtocol, the compiler turns for-try-await into repeated next() calls, and the standard library's flatMap returns an AsyncFlatMapSequence that flattens a sequence of sequences lazily - so a composite becomes a stream of parts without any Splitter type. The proposal that introduced the protocol uses exactly this shape (URL.lines() consumed with for try await line), and single-value algorithms such as contains/first/reduce are provided for the consumer side. For an in-memory array, Sequence.flatMap/compactMap suffices; the role structure reappears only when the parts must be handed to a transport, where the for-await loop becomes the send loop and cancellation is handled with the Task API.
pitfalls: After next() returns nil (or throws) every later call must keep returning nil - an iterator that restarts breaks for-await and any consumer that re-checks completion.
Long-running part production must observe Task.isCancelled, otherwise a cancelled consumer waits forever for the next element.
Sequence.flatMap and AsyncSequence.flatMap differ in laziness: the synchronous one on a large collection materialises eagerly, the asynchronous one is demand-driven.
